content: 1. The President of the Latin American Association for Palliative Care (ALCP) is actively working to enhance global access to palliative care. This individual has received funding from the International Association for Hospice and Palliative Care (IAHPC), which is in official relations with the World Health Organization (WHO), to volunteer at WHO headquarters. They are considered to have no significant conflicts of interest, and no conflict management measures are required. 2. Nguyen Thi Phuong Cham, a retired senior pharmaceutical expert and consultant for the Vietnam Administration of Medical Services under the Ministry of Health, has contributed to palliative care by providing training on pain policy for physicians and hospital administrators in Vietnam. This work, conducted in collaboration with the Pain and Policy Studies Group, was deemed significant in April 2012. Additionally, she has been involved in training programs on the rational use of drugs, including activities of Drug Therapy Committees and pharmacology, as a volunteer for the Ministry of Health from April 2012 to 2017. Her work also included assessing the quality of diagnosis and prescriptions in hospitals supported by the GIZ project, which was considered significant in August 2016. She is regarded as having no significant conflicts of interest, and no conflict management measures are required. 3. A clinical psychologist with a diploma in clinical psychology and a member of the Associate Fellow of the British Psychological Society (AFBPS) has been serving as the President of the German Association for Palliative Medicine since 2014. They also hold the position of Chairman of the Board of Directors of the International Association for Hospice and Palliative Care (IAHPC). They are considered to have no significant conflicts of interest, and no conflict management measures are required. 4. The WHO Guidelines Development Group (GDG) ensured transparency by requiring all members to complete a Declaration of Interests (DOI) form before the initial scoping and guideline formulation meetings. Any reported conflicts of interest were reviewed by the guidelines coordinator and the responsible technical officer. In five cases of potentially significant conflicts of interest, advice was sought from the Secretariat of the Guidelines Review Committee and WHO’s Department of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics (CRE). Actions taken included exclusion from the GDG, exclusion from specific topic areas, or exclusion from final voting on recommendations. The final decision to exclude these individuals was made by the Director of the Department for Management of Noncommunicable Diseases, Disability, Violence, and Injury Prevention (NVI), based on advice from the Steering Group and CRE colleagues. 5. GDG members were instructed to update their DOI forms throughout the process and notify the responsible technical officer and guidelines coordinator of any relevant changes. Individuals with roles in pharmaceutical companies, such as owners, co-owners, or advisory board members, were excluded from the External Review Group (ERG) and GDG membership. Memberships and directorships of professional bodies were evaluated for potential conflicts of interest, as were the funding sources of these organizations. All GDG members were required to share their curricula vitae, and brief biographies of potential members were published on the WHO website from June to September 2016. 6. WHO policies on conflicts of interest were fully applied throughout the guideline development process. Relevant declared conflicts of interest and the strategies employed to manage them were reported in the guidelines publication. A standing agenda item on Conflicts of Interests was included at the beginning of all GDG meetings, where declared conflicts were presented to the entire group. 7. The WHO guidelines for the pharmacological and radiotherapeutic management of cancer pain in adults and adolescents emphasize the importance of balancing access to opioid analgesics for medical needs while minimizing the risk of misuse. The guidelines provide an overview of international conventions governing the procurement, distribution, and dispensing of opioid medicines, particularly under the United Nations Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961. 8. The Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961, as amended by the 1972 Protocol, is the principal international treaty regulating the control of opioids. It aims to limit the production, manufacture, exportation, importation, distribution, trade, use, and possession of narcotic drugs exclusively for medical and scientific purposes. Morphine and other strong opioids, such as fentanyl, hydromorphone, oxycodone, and methadone, are listed under Schedule I of the convention. 9. Countries that are parties to the Single Convention are required to estimate their annual medical and scientific requirements for Schedule I narcotic drugs and submit these estimates to the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB) for confirmation. The quantities manufactured or imported must not exceed these estimates. Governments must also ensure that controlled substances remain in the hands of licensed parties, require medical prescriptions for dispensing, and maintain a system of inspection to prevent diversion and abuse. 10. The INCB has observed significant disparities in global access to opioid analgesics. For example, six developed countries account for 79% of global morphine consumption, while developing countries, representing 80% of the world’s population, account for only 6%. This disparity highlights the need for balanced national policies that ensure adequate access to opioids for medical purposes while preventing misuse. 11. Governments are encouraged to review their drug control legislation and policies to identify overly restrictive provisions that hinder the delivery of appropriate medical care involving controlled medicines. They should aim to optimize health outcomes and take corrective action as needed. Decisions regarding medical use of controlled substances should be made by health professionals, guided by WHO policy guidelines, such as Ensuring balance in national policies on controlled substances. 12. Competent national authorities, designated under the Single Convention, are responsible for liaising with the INCB and administering national regulations related to controlled substances for medical use. These authorities are typically located within the national medicines regulatory authority or the Ministry of Health. In some countries, they may be separate government agencies or offices within other ministries, such as justice, police, or finance. 13. National authorities must prepare annual estimates of their requirements for Schedule I narcotic drugs and submit them to the INCB by June 30 for the following calendar year. These estimates set the yearly limits for the procurement of strong opioids for medical use. Exporting countries will refuse to supply additional narcotic substances to a country that has exceeded its official estimates. Therefore, accurate submission of estimates is crucial for ensuring the availability of controlled substances for medical and scientific purposes.
